lesson.title: Believing People Get What They Deserve
lesson.summary: The just-world phenomenon is the tendency to believe that the world is fundamentally fair, that people generally get what they deserve, a comforting belief that can also lead people to blame innocent victims for their own misfortune.
lesson.body:
Psychologist Melvin Lerner developed the just-world hypothesis starting in the mid-1960s, describing a widespread motivational need to believe that the world is orderly, predictable, and fair, that good things happen to good people and bad things happen to people who somehow brought it on themselves. This belief is comforting for an obvious reason. If the world is truly just, then bad fortune is avoidable, and a person can feel safer simply by being a good, careful, deserving person. The uncomfortable flip side is what happens when we witness something that clashes with this belief: an innocent person suffering for no fault of their own.

In a classic 1966 study, Lerner and his colleague Carolyn Simmons had participants watch a woman apparently receiving painful electric shocks as part of what was described as a learning experiment. The woman had done nothing to deserve this treatment. When participants had no ability to help her or compensate her for her suffering, many of them responded not with straightforward sympathy but by derogating her, rating her as less likable and implying that something about her character explained what was happening to her. This was, in effect, a way of resolving the uncomfortable clash between the world is fair and an innocent person is suffering right in front of me and I cannot do anything about it, by quietly deciding she must deserve it somehow after all.

This connects directly back to attribution theory, and specifically echoes the fundamental attribution error from the start of this unit, though aimed at victims rather than at ordinary behavior. Instead of correctly attributing someone's misfortune to chance, circumstance, or another person's wrongdoing, all situational causes, just-world thinking nudges observers toward a dispositional attribution instead, toward believing something about the victim's own choices or character caused their suffering. The mechanism is related but the motivation is sharper and more specific: this is not just a passive perceptual bias, it is an active, motivated attempt to preserve a comforting belief about fairness that feels threatened by the victim's undeserved suffering.

This kind of judgment also tends to operate implicitly, much like the automatic associations discussed in the previous chapter. People rarely reason consciously, deciding to blame a victim in order to protect their belief in a just world. Instead, the victim blaming judgment tends to arise quickly and gets rationalized only afterward, if at all. Understanding the just-world phenomenon helps explain the persistence of victim blaming aimed at survivors of poverty, sexual assault, and serious illness, questions like what did they do to deserve this, or could they have prevented it, and it is a reminder that reducing prejudice and unfair judgment, discussed earlier in this unit through ideas like Allport's contact hypothesis, has to contend with these deep motivational pulls toward believing the world is fairer than it actually is, not simply with correcting inaccurate facts about groups of people.
